6 Localization of Validity, Failure, and Approximation

← Previous chapterChapter 5: Generation of Observer Time at the Dynamical-Description Stage→ Next chapterChapter 7: Audit of Law-Time Use and Nonachievement of Primitive-Time PremisesContents

Take as input the complete evaluation specification of Definition 5.2. Validity and failure localization specifies the invalidating conditions and their dependencies for the comparison, representation, continuum-approximation, dynamical-description, law-representation, and differential-consistency and law-form-preservation series, and generates a six-series failure signature, scale boundaries, and operational audit data. Engineering audit parameters provide the formal evidence used to evaluate failure in each series.

In what follows, only within a local context in which a single complete evaluation specification is fixed, each symbol root is first displayed in full in its first formula, after which the subscript pair formed by the second and third components uniquely recoverable from that complete evaluation specification is omitted. Independent identifiers are not omitted, and the component pair is not omitted when multiple complete evaluation specifications are treated simultaneously.

6.1 Basic Definitions of Validity Domains and Localization

Definition 6.1 (Validity localization).

For a set

AA

and a binary predicate

P:A⟶{⊥,⊤}P:A\longrightarrow\{\bot\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\top\}

define its validity localization by

ValA⁡(P):={a∈A∣P⁢[a]=⊤}\operatorname{Val}_{A}(P):=\{a\in A\mid P[a]=\top\}

Further, for a set

BB

and a binary predicate

Q:B×A⟶{⊥,⊤}Q:B\times A\longrightarrow\{\bot\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\top\}

b∈Bb\in B

into its first argument by

ValA⁡(Q;b):={a∈A∣Q⁢[b;a]=⊤}\operatorname{Val}_{A}(Q;b):=\{a\in A\mid Q[b;a]=\top\}

Suppose that a set of complete evaluation specifications

𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼,\mathsf{EvSpec}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak

a condition-index set

II

and a family of binary condition predicates

Ki:𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⟶{⊥,⊤},i∈IK_{i}:\mathsf{EvSpec}\longrightarrow\{\bot\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\top\}% \mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad i\in I

are given. For any

J⊆IJ\subseteq I

define

Val𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⁡((Ki)i∈J)\displaystyle\operatorname{Val}_{\mathsf{EvSpec}}\bigl{(}(K_{i})_{i\in J}\bigr% {)} :={𝖤𝗏∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼∣∀i∈J,Ki⁢[𝖤𝗏]=⊤}\displaystyle:=\{\mathsf{Ev}\in\mathsf{EvSpec}\mid\forall i\in J\mathchar 44% \relax\allowbreak\ K_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}]=\top\}
=⋂i∈JVal𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⁡(Ki)\displaystyle=\bigcap_{i\in J}\operatorname{Val}_{\mathsf{EvSpec}}(K_{i})

Let the strict establishment condition and the approximation establishment condition be

K𝗌𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖼𝗍fail\displaystyle K_{\mathsf{strict}}^{\mathrm{fail}} :𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⟶{⊥,⊤},\displaystyle:\mathsf{EvSpec}\longrightarrow\{\bot\mathchar 44\relax% \allowbreak\top\}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail\displaystyle K_{\mathsf{approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}} :𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ⟶{⊥,⊤}\displaystyle:\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}\longrightarrow\{\bot\mathchar 44\relax% \allowbreak\top\}

respectively. By Definition 6.1, define

𝒱strict\displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{strict}} :=Val𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⁡(K𝗌𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖼𝗍fail),\displaystyle:=\operatorname{Val}_{\mathsf{EvSpec}}\left(K_{\mathsf{strict}}^{% \mathrm{fail}}\right)\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝒱approx\displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{approx}} :=Val𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ⁡(K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail),\displaystyle:=\operatorname{Val}_{\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}}\left(K_{\mathsf{% approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}}\right)\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝒱full\displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{full}} :=(𝒱strict×Λ)∩𝒱approx\displaystyle:=\left(\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{strict}}\times\Lambda\right)\cap% \mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{approx}}

and call these the strict validity domain, approximation validity domain, and full-evaluation validity domain, respectively.

Lemma 6.5 (Inclusion maximum of a family of sets).

For a set

AA

and a family of sets

𝔄⊆𝒫⁢(A)\mathfrak{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(A)

a necessary and sufficient condition for

Max⊆⁡𝔄\operatorname{Max}_{\subseteq}\mathfrak{A}

to exist is

⋃B∈𝔄B∈𝔄\bigcup_{B\in\mathfrak{A}}B\in\mathfrak{A}

In this case,

Max⊆⁡𝔄=⋃B∈𝔄B\operatorname{Max}_{\subseteq}\mathfrak{A}=\bigcup_{B\in\mathfrak{A}}B

and the maximum element is unique.

Proof.

If a maximum element

Bmax∈𝔄B^{\max}\in\mathfrak{A}

exists, every

B∈𝔄B\in\mathfrak{A}

satisfies

B⊆BmaxB\subseteq B^{\max}

and

⋃B∈𝔄B=Bmax∈𝔄.\bigcup_{B\in\mathfrak{A}}B=B^{\max}\in\mathfrak{A}.

Conversely, if this union belongs to

𝔄\mathfrak{A}

then it is a maximum element containing every member. Uniqueness follows from antisymmetry of set inclusion. ∎

𝒱max=Max⊆⁡𝔙adm⁢(𝒱)\mathcal{V}^{\max}=\operatorname{Max}_{\subseteq}\mathfrak{V}_{\mathrm{adm}}(% \mathcal{V})

A necessary and sufficient condition for the maximum validity domain to exist is

⋃𝒱′∈𝔙adm⁢(𝒱)𝒱′∈𝔙adm⁢(𝒱)\bigcup_{\mathcal{V}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{V}_{\mathrm{adm}}(\mathcal{V})}% \mathcal{V}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{V}_{\mathrm{adm}}(\mathcal{V})

and it is unique.

Apply Lemma 6.5 to

A=𝒱,𝔄=𝔙adm⁢(𝒱)A=\mathcal{V}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{V}_{% \mathrm{adm}}(\mathcal{V})

∎

Definition 6.8 (Maximal effective interval).

For a totally ordered set

(Λ,≤Λ)(\Lambda\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\leq_{\Lambda})

and a subset

B⊆ΛB\subseteq\Lambda

define the family of initial subsets contained in that subset by

InitΛ⁡(B):={ℐ⊆B|∀μ∈ℐ,∀λ∈Λ,λ≤Λμ⟹λ∈ℐ}\operatorname{Init}_{\Lambda}(B):=\left\{\mathcal{I}\subseteq B\ \middle|\ % \forall\mu\in\mathcal{I}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\ \forall\lambda\in% \Lambda\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\ \lambda\leq_{\Lambda}\mu\Longrightarrow% \lambda\in\mathcal{I}\right\}

For each

𝖤𝗏∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Ev}\in\mathsf{EvSpec}

define the family of admissible initial intervals by

ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]:=InitΛ⁡(ValΛ⁡(K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail;𝖤𝗏))\mathfrak{I}_{\mathrm{init}}[\mathsf{Ev}]:=\operatorname{Init}_{\Lambda}\left(% \operatorname{Val}_{\Lambda}\left(K_{\mathsf{approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}};\mathsf{% Ev}\right)\right)

The object

ℐmax⁢[𝖤𝗏]=Max⊆⁡ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathcal{I}^{\max}[\mathsf{Ev}]=\operatorname{Max}_{\subseteq}\mathfrak{I}_{% \mathrm{init}}[\mathsf{Ev}]

is called the maximal effective interval at

𝖤𝗏\mathsf{Ev}
Proposition 6.9 (Existence of the maximal effective interval).

For any complete evaluation specification 𝖤𝗏∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Ev}\in\mathsf{EvSpec}, the maximal effective interval exists uniquely, and

⋃ℐ∈ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]ℐ∈ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]\bigcup_{\mathcal{I}\in\mathfrak{I}_{\mathrm{init}}[\mathsf{Ev}]}\mathcal{I}% \in\mathfrak{I}_{\mathrm{init}}[\mathsf{Ev}]

Further, if the scale-monotonicity condition

∀λ,μ∈Λ,λ≤Λμ∧K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail[𝖤𝗏;μ]=⊤⟹K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail[λ]=⊤\forall\lambda\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\mu\in\Lambda\mathchar 44\relax% \allowbreak\quad\lambda\leq_{\Lambda}\mu\ \wedge K_{\mathsf{approx}}^{\mathrm{% fail}}[\mathsf{Ev};\mu]=\top\Longrightarrow K_{\mathsf{approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}% }[\lambda]=\top

holds, then

ℐmax⁢[𝖤𝗏]=ValΛ⁡(K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail;𝖤𝗏)\mathcal{I}^{\max}[\mathsf{Ev}]=\operatorname{Val}_{\Lambda}\left(K_{\mathsf{% approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}};\mathsf{Ev}\right)

and it is unique. Its maximum endpoint exists if and only if

Max⁡(ℐmax⁢[𝖤𝗏])\operatorname{Max}\left(\mathcal{I}^{\max}[\mathsf{Ev}]\right)

exists.

Proof.

Because the empty set belongs to

ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathfrak{I}_{\mathrm{init}}[\mathsf{Ev}]

this family is nonempty. Its union is also an initial subset contained in the approximation-validity domain and therefore belongs to the same family. Applying Lemma 6.5 to

A=Λ,𝔄=ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]A=\Lambda\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{I}_{\mathrm% {init}}[\mathsf{Ev}]

yields existence and uniqueness of the maximal effective interval.

Under the scale-monotonicity condition, the approximation localization of Definition 6.2 is itself an admissible initial interval and contains all of its members. It therefore coincides with the maximal effective interval. The assertion concerning the maximum endpoint follows from the definition. ∎

Iτfail\displaystyle I_{\tau}^{\mathrm{fail}} :={1,…,nτfail},\displaystyle:=\{1\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\ldots\mathchar 44\relax% \allowbreak n_{\tau}^{\mathrm{fail}}\}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼τ\displaystyle\mathsf{FailSpec}_{\tau} :={𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼,τ∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖾𝗌strict,𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ,τ=𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑\displaystyle:=\begin{cases}\mathsf{EvSpec}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak&\tau% \in\mathsf{FailSeries}^{\mathrm{strict}}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\\ \mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak&\tau=\mathsf{approx}% \end{cases}

Lemma 6.16 (Reachability order of rank-increasing edges).

Suppose that a set

V,V\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak

an edge set

E⊆V×V,E\subseteq V\times V\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak

a strict partially ordered set

(R,<R)(R\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak<_{R})

and a map

r:V⟶Rr:V\longrightarrow R

satisfy

(v,w)∈E⟹r⁢(v)<Rr⁢(w)(v\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak w)\in E\Longrightarrow r(v)<_{R}r(w)

Write the relation given by equality or by the existence of a positive-length finite directed path on

EE

as

⪯E\preceq_{E}

Then

EE

has no directed cycle, and

⪯E\preceq_{E}

is a partial order on

VV
Proof.

Equality gives reflexivity, and concatenation of directed paths gives transitivity. Because

rr

increases strictly along every directed path, a directed cycle would imply

r⁢(v)<Rr⁢(v)r(v)<_{R}r(v)

contrary to the irreflexivity of a strict partial order. Two distinct points reachable from one another in both directions would yield a directed cycle, so antisymmetry also holds. ∎

Proposition 6.22 (Existence and uniqueness of the evaluation-state assignment and decomposition into state fibers).

There exists exactly one evaluation-state map

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖮𝖿:𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖠𝗋𝗀⟶𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾\mathsf{FailStateOf}:\mathsf{FailEvalArg}\longrightarrow\mathsf{FailState}

that satisfies the recursive conditions of Definition 6.21. For each

(𝖤𝗏,λ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ(\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda)\in\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}

the family

{𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖥𝗂𝖻𝖾𝗋q⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]|q∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾}\left\{\mathsf{FailFiber}_{q}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda]\ \middle|\ q\in\mathsf{% FailState}\right\}

gives a decomposition into pairwise disjoint state fibers of

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄.\mathsf{FailTok}.

Empty state fibers are allowed. Its restrictions to

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄strict,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄approx\mathsf{FailTok}^{\mathrm{strict}}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad\mathsf{% FailTok}^{\mathrm{approx}}

give decompositions of the respective subsets into pairwise disjoint state fibers.

Proof.

By Propositions 6.15 and 6.18,

(𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖤𝖽𝗀𝖾)(\mathsf{FailTok}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{FailEdge})

is a finite directed acyclic graph. At each token, the four branches of Definition 6.21 return exactly one state from the family of direct-predecessor states, the two input-satisfaction values, and the failure-condition evaluation value. Lemma 6.20 therefore gives the existence and uniqueness of the evaluation-state map.

Because each token has exactly one of the four states, the four state fibers are pairwise disjoint. Their union equals

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{FailTok}

and their restrictions to either of the two series-side subsets remain pairwise disjoint and exhaustive. ∎

For any

(𝖤𝗏,λ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄τ,i∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄(\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda)\in\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}% \mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad\mathsf{FailTok}_{\tau\mathchar 44\relax% \allowbreak i}\in\mathsf{FailTok}

one has

Furthermore,

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[λ]\displaystyle\mathsf{FailedTok}[\lambda] =𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄strict⁢[𝖤𝗏]⊔𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄approx⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ],\displaystyle=\mathsf{FailedTok}^{\mathrm{strict}}[\mathsf{Ev}]\sqcup\mathsf{% FailedTok}^{\mathrm{approx}}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda]\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄strict⁢[𝖤𝗏]\displaystyle\mathsf{FailedTok}^{\mathrm{strict}}[\mathsf{Ev}] =𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[λ]∩𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄strict,\displaystyle=\mathsf{FailedTok}[\lambda]\cap\mathsf{FailTok}^{\mathrm{strict}% }\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄approx⁢[λ]\displaystyle\mathsf{FailedTok}^{\mathrm{approx}}[\lambda] =𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[λ]∩𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄approx\displaystyle=\mathsf{FailedTok}[\lambda]\cap\mathsf{FailTok}^{\mathrm{approx}}

and all three sets are finite.

Proof.

The equivalence and the three displays follow from Definition 6.21. By Proposition 6.15,

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{FailTok}

is finite, and the three sets are its subsets. ∎

Definition 6.24 (Strict failure-generation dependency order and three cases of minimal failure).

s≺𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝖽𝖾𝗉t⟺s⪯𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝖽𝖾𝗉t∧s≠ts\prec^{\mathsf{fail\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak dep}}t\quad% \Longleftrightarrow\quad s\preceq^{\mathsf{fail\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak dep% }}t\ \wedge\ s\neq t

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖢𝖺𝗌𝖾𝖮𝖿⁢(𝖤𝗏;λ)\displaystyle\mathsf{FailCaseOf}(\mathsf{Ev};\lambda) :={𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖠𝖻𝗌𝖾𝗇𝗍,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖢𝗈𝗎𝗇𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]=0,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖴𝗇𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖢𝗈𝗎𝗇𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]=1,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗅𝗅𝖾𝗅,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖢𝗈𝗎𝗇𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]≥2\displaystyle:=\begin{cases}\mathsf{FailAbsent}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak&% \mathsf{FailCount}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda]=0\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\\ \mathsf{FailUnique}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak&\mathsf{FailCount}[\mathsf{Ev% };\lambda]=1\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\\ \mathsf{FailParallel}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak&\mathsf{FailCount}[\mathsf{% Ev};\lambda]\geq 2\end{cases}

Lemma 6.25 (Forward propagation of a nonsatisfied state into unformed successors).

Take an evaluation specification

(𝖤𝗏,λ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ(\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda)\in\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}

ar:=𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖠𝗋𝗀𝖠𝗍𝖤𝗏,λ⁢(tr)a_{r}:=\mathsf{FailArgAt}_{\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda}(t_% {r})

one has

For every

r≥1r\geq 1

The initial state is not satisfied, and at each inductive step the immediately preceding state satisfies

in succession. ∎

Proposition 6.26 (Incomparability of failed tokens, equality with the minimal elements, and the three cases).

For any

(𝖤𝗏,λ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ(\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda)\in\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}

and distinct

one has

s∥𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝖽𝖾𝗉⁢t.s\parallel_{\mathsf{fail\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak dep}}t.

Consequently,

Min⪯𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝖽𝖾𝗉⁡𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[λ]=𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[λ].\operatorname{Min}_{\preceq^{\mathsf{fail\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak dep}}}% \mathsf{FailedTok}[\lambda]=\mathsf{FailedTok}[\lambda].

Moreover,

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖢𝖺𝗌𝖾𝖮𝖿⁢(𝖤𝗏;λ)\mathsf{FailCaseOf}(\mathsf{Ev};\lambda)

is uniquely determined as one of the following three cases:

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖠𝖻𝗌𝖾𝗇𝗍,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖴𝗇𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗅𝗅𝖾𝗅\mathsf{FailAbsent}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad\mathsf{FailUnique}% \mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad\mathsf{FailParallel}
Proof.

Suppose first that the relation

s≺𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝖽𝖾𝗉ts\prec^{\mathsf{fail\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak dep}}t

holds. There then exists a positive-length directed path described by

s=t0⟶⋯⟶tm=ts=t_{0}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow t_{m}=t

Proposition 6.23 then implies that the state at its initial point is

𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽≠𝗌𝖺𝗍.\mathsf{failed}\neq\mathsf{sat}.

By Lemma 6.25, the state at the endpoint is

𝗎𝗇𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖾𝖽\mathsf{unformed}

whereas, by the same proposition, the state of

t∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]t\in\mathsf{FailedTok}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda]

is

𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽\mathsf{failed}

and this contradicts uniqueness of the state.

Conversely, suppose that t≺𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅,𝖽𝖾𝗉st\prec^{\mathsf{fail\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak dep}}s. The state at the initial point tt is 𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽\mathsf{failed}, and Lemma 6.25 implies that the state at the endpoint ss is 𝗎𝗇𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖾𝖽\mathsf{unformed}. On the other hand, s∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[λ]s\in\mathsf{FailedTok}[\lambda] implies that the state of ss is 𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽\mathsf{failed}, again contradicting uniqueness of the state. Distinct elements of the failed set are therefore incomparable in both directions. Hence the failed set is an antichain and every element is minimal.

Because the failed set is finite, its cardinality falls into exactly one of the following three classes:

0,1,2⁢ or more0\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad 1\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad 2% \text{ or more}

and Definition 6.24 gives the three cases. ∎

and set

𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖱𝖾𝗀=(⨆λ∈𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖨𝖽𝗑(ρ)𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖱𝖾𝗀λ(ρ))⊔𝖴𝗇𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖽𝖱𝖾𝗀(ρ).\mathsf{ParentReg}=\left(\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\mathsf{SubIdx}^{(\rho)}}\mathsf% {SubReg}^{(\rho)}_{\lambda}\right)\sqcup\mathsf{UnrefinedReg}^{(\rho)}.

𝖢𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝖾𝖽𝖱𝖾𝗀(0)\displaystyle\mathsf{CoveredReg}^{(0)} ⊆𝖢𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝖾𝖽𝖱𝖾𝗀(1),\displaystyle\subseteq\mathsf{CoveredReg}^{(1)}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝖴𝗇𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖽𝖱𝖾𝗀(1)\displaystyle\mathsf{UnrefinedReg}^{(1)} ⊆𝖴𝗇𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖽𝖱𝖾𝗀(0).\displaystyle\subseteq\mathsf{UnrefinedReg}^{(0)}.

Each covered region is a subset of the parent region, and the unrefined region is the set difference obtained by removing the covered region from the parent region. The two regions are therefore disjoint, and their union equals the parent region. If the family of subregions is pairwise disjoint, replacing the union in the covered region by a disjoint union gives the second decomposition.

Every subregion indexed by the first index set is contained in the second covering union because the two families agree on their common indices. This proves the inclusion between the covered regions. Removing the covered regions from the same parent region reverses that inclusion, which proves the inclusion between the unrefined regions. ∎

6.4 Failure positions at the representation stage

The three representation-stage conditions in Definition 4.92 are placed in correspondence with the three representation failure-position tokens in Definition 6.10. Representation-stage failure is classified by the first failure position among the three conditions on the domain in which comparison-stage operativeness holds.

Satisfaction of the dynamical series expresses satisfaction of all direct predecessors outside the approximation series; this input condition does not include satisfaction of the nine conditions within the approximation series.

Proposition 6.76 (Generation dependencies of the nine continuum-approximation conditions).

By the within-series dependency edges of the continuum-approximation series in Definition 6.17, the six first-layer conditions are mutually incomparable. Within the first layer, satisfaction of one condition is not a prerequisite for evaluation readiness of another.

The direct-predecessor set of the continuous-extension condition is the token set of the six first-layer conditions. The direct-predecessor sets of the order-stability and relation-stability conditions consist of the token for the continuous-extension condition.

By the between-series dependency edges in Definition 6.17, every token in the dynamical-description series is a direct predecessor of each continuum-approximation condition. Consequently, the evaluation state in Definition 6.21 is uniquely determined by the satisfaction states of the comparison, representation, and dynamical-description series; the direct-predecessor conditions within the continuum-approximation series; the non-ancestor formative-input satisfaction value; and the evaluation-input satisfaction value.

By Definition 6.90 and Definition 6.88, membership in the saturation index set is equivalent to a zero margin and to equality of the defect quantity and the tolerance, whereas membership in the excess index set is equivalent to a positive excess, a negative margin, and exceedance of the tolerance by the defect quantity.

hold. Therefore λ𝖻𝖽𝗋𝗒approx⁢[𝖤𝗏]\lambda_{\mathsf{bdry}}^{\mathrm{approx}}[\mathsf{Ev}] is the least approximation scale at which an excess component occurs.

Proof.

Take μ∈𝒱𝖤𝗏approx\mu\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{Ev}}^{\mathrm{approx}} and λ≤Λμ\lambda\leq_{\Lambda}\mu. For each i∈I𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑faili\in I_{\mathsf{approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}}, scale validity and monotonic nondecrease give

Hence λ∈𝒱𝖤𝗏approx\lambda\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{Ev}}^{\mathrm{approx}}, and this scale validity domain is an initial segment.

In Definition 6.93, the scale validity domain itself belongs to ℑinit⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathfrak{I}_{\mathrm{init}}[\mathsf{Ev}], and every member of that family is contained in the scale validity domain. Hence the union of the family equals the scale validity domain, and each initial segment is contained in that union. If a greatest element λin\lambda_{\mathrm{in}} exists, it belongs to the scale validity domain; Theorem 6.95 then gives an empty excess index set.

Under the assumption in the latter part, Definition 6.86 and Definition 6.4 identify the scale validity domain with ValΛ⁡(K𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑fail;𝖤𝗏)\operatorname{Val}_{\Lambda}(K_{\mathsf{approx}}^{\mathrm{fail}};\mathsf{Ev}). Proposition 6.31 gives the initial-interval representation of the maximal effective interval. By Definition 6.29, the boundary scale lies outside the scale validity domain, while every smaller scale belongs to the maximal effective interval. Applying Theorem 6.95 to the boundary scale and to each lower scale gives, respectively, nonemptiness and emptiness of the excess index set. Thus the boundary scale is the least scale at which an excess component occurs. ∎

Proof.

Suppose failure at the law-description stage holds. By Definition 6.111, the complete evaluation specification belongs to the law-description-stage failure domain. Proposition 6.116 then shows that the corresponding simultaneous minimal-failure node set is nonempty.

Definition 6.115 gives a minimal failure class at the law-description stage corresponding to some law-failure index. Definition 6.114 gives dynamical-description operability and a false value for the corresponding law-condition evaluation. By Definition 6.109, the simultaneous satisfaction of all law conditions fails; Definition 6.110 then establishes failure at the law-description stage.

Definition 6.115 also shows that nonemptiness of the simultaneous minimal-failure node set is equivalent to the occurrence of a minimal failure class at the law-description stage corresponding to some law-failure index, and hence to a disjunction over the finite index set. The three conditions in the proposition are therefore equivalent.

The equivalence for every complete evaluation specification, together with Definition 6.111, gives the set equality for the failure domain.

Suppose that the simultaneous minimal-failure node set at the law-description stage has at least two elements. By Definition 6.115, the minimal failure class at the law-description stage corresponding to each node in the set holds. Proposition 6.116 shows that these nodes form an antichain in the law-condition dependency directed acyclic graph. ∎

Proposition 6.118 (Stage Separation of Failure at the Dynamical-Description and Law-Description Stages).

For each 𝖤𝗏=(𝖨,o,ζ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Ev}=(\mathsf{I}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak o\mathchar 44\relax% \allowbreak\zeta)\in\mathsf{EvSpec},

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖽𝗒𝗇⁢[𝖤𝗏]\displaystyle\mathsf{Fail}_{\mathsf{dyn}}[\mathsf{Ev}] ⟹¬𝖣𝗒𝗇𝖮𝗉𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗏𝖾⁢[𝖤𝗏],\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\neg\mathsf{DynOperative}[\mathsf{Ev}]\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak
𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝗅𝖺𝗐⁢[𝖤𝗏]\displaystyle\mathsf{Fail}_{\mathsf{law}}[\mathsf{Ev}] ⟹𝖣𝗒𝗇𝖮𝗉𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗏𝖾⁢[𝖤𝗏]\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\mathsf{DynOperative}[\mathsf{Ev}]

hold. Consequently,

¬(𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖽𝗒𝗇⁢[𝖤𝗏]∧𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝗅𝖺𝗐⁢[𝖤𝗏])\neg\left(\mathsf{Fail}_{\mathsf{dyn}}[\mathsf{Ev}]\wedge\mathsf{Fail}_{% \mathsf{law}}[\mathsf{Ev}]\right)

holds.

Proof.

By Definitions 6.104 and 6.102, if 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖽𝗒𝗇⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{Fail}_{\mathsf{dyn}}[\mathsf{Ev}] holds, then for some i∈I𝖽𝗒𝗇faili\in I_{\mathsf{dyn}}^{\mathrm{fail}},

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖮𝖿⁢(𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄𝖽𝗒𝗇,i;Γ𝖤𝗏dyn)=𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽\displaystyle\mathsf{FailStateOf}\left(\mathsf{FailTok}_{\mathsf{dyn}\mathchar 4% 4\relax\allowbreak i};\Gamma^{\mathrm{dyn}}_{\mathsf{Ev}}\right)=\mathsf{failed}

holds. Proposition 6.101 gives Kidyn⁢[𝖤𝗏]=⊥.K_{i}^{\mathrm{dyn}}[\mathsf{Ev}]=\bot. Definition 6.100 then gives ¬𝖣𝗒𝗇𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝖠𝗅𝗅⁢[𝖤𝗏]\neg\mathsf{DynCondAll}[\mathsf{Ev}]. By Definition 5.70, ¬𝖣𝗒𝗇𝖮𝗉𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗏𝖾⁢[𝖤𝗏]\neg\mathsf{DynOperative}\left[\mathsf{Ev}\right] holds.

The equivalence in Proposition 6.112 implies that failure at the law-description stage entails dynamical-description operability. Dynamical-description operability is incompatible with the negation of dynamical-description operability obtained from failure at the dynamical-description stage. The two failures therefore cannot hold simultaneously, and the final conclusion of the proposition follows. ∎

For each law-failure index, if the domain of the corresponding minimal failure class is nonempty, the selected 𝖤𝗏iwit∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖶𝗂𝗍𝗅𝖺𝗐\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{wit}}_{i}\in\mathsf{FailWit}_{\mathsf{law}} satisfies 𝖥𝖫i⁢[𝖤𝗏iwit]\mathsf{FL}_{i}\left[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{wit}}_{i}\right].

Thus, for each minimal failure class, the equivalence stated in the proposition holds between nonemptiness of the class and the existence of a selected witness corresponding to that class. ∎

Furthermore, if two child-region families for the same parent region satisfy the inclusion condition and the agreement condition on common indices in Lemma 6.33, then the covered region after refinement contains the covered region before refinement, and the unrefined region after refinement is contained in the unrefined region before refinement.

Proof.

Each child region satisfies 𝖫𝖺𝗐𝖯𝗎𝗋𝖾𝖢𝖺𝗌𝖾i,σ\mathsf{LawPureCase}_{i\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\sigma}. Because two distinct types at the same node cannot both be pure types, the family of child regions is mutually exclusive. Definition 6.129 and Theorem 6.35 give the disjoint-union representation of the covered region and the decomposition of the parent region.

The unrefined remainder representation is established node by node. At node 1, at least one of the two individual-law application-domain counterexample types occurs on the parent region. Belonging to neither pure-type region is equivalent to the occurrence of both types.

At node 2, nonuniqueness of a candidate-output fiber occurs on the parent region. Being outside the output-conflict-on-generated-evaluation-arguments subregion is equivalent to the existence of a nonunique candidate-output fiber and to the candidate-output fiber containing at most one element at every generated evaluation argument that belongs to the evaluation domain. This is 𝖫𝖺𝗐𝖮𝖿𝖿𝖦𝖾𝗇𝖠𝗋𝗀𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖿𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{LawOffGenArgConflict}[\mathsf{Ev}].

At node 3, a generated law-evaluation relation-membership counterexample occurs on the parent region, and its candidate-output fiber is either empty or nonempty. Belonging to neither pure-type region is equivalent to the occurrence of counterexamples belonging to both fiber types.

At node 4, a counterexample to the faithful-representation-transformation invariance of candidate-relation membership occurs on the parent region. The two distinct membership-indicator values are either (1,0)(1\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak 0) or (0,1)(0\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak 1). Belonging to neither pure-type region is equivalent to the occurrence of both a membership-loss counterexample and a membership-gain counterexample.

At node 5, exactly one of the following holds: the common valid time domain is empty, or it is nonempty and inadmissible. Every element of the parent region therefore belongs to one pure-type child region, and the unrefined remainder region is empty.

Substituting these results into Definition 6.128 gives the unrefined remainder representation and the two identities for node 5. The final two inclusions follow by applying Lemma 6.33 to the root nodes of the law-failure counterexample refinement forest. ∎

By Definition 5.132, differential-stage operability is equivalent to the conjunction of law-description operability and the full differential-condition bundle. Thus, under law-description operability, the negation of differential-stage operability is equivalent to the negation of the full differential-condition bundle. By Definition 6.137, this equivalence gives the equivalence stated in the proposition. ∎

6.8.4 Failure-Domain Cover Relative to the Differential-Condition DAG

Theorem 6.145 (Failure-domain cover relative to the differential-condition DAG).

Take a set 𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{EvSpec} of complete evaluation specifications. Relative to the five universal differential conditions and the differential-condition DAG of Definition 5.130,

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖣𝗈𝗆diff⁢(𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼)\displaystyle\mathsf{FailDom}_{\mathrm{diff}}\left(\mathsf{EvSpec}\right)
=⋃i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖱𝖾𝗀diff,i⁢(𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼).\displaystyle=\bigcup_{i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}}\mathsf{FailReg}% _{\mathrm{diff}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak i}\left(\mathsf{EvSpec}\right).

Equivalently, for each 𝖤𝗏∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Ev}\in\mathsf{EvSpec},

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅diff⁢[𝖤𝗏]\displaystyle\mathsf{Fail}_{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}]
⟺⋁i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond𝖥𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿i⁢[𝖤𝗏].\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\bigvee_{i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}% }}\mathsf{FDiff}_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}].

Members of this cover may intersect at evaluation specifications containing simultaneous minimal-failure nodes.

Proof.

First take any evaluation specification 𝖤𝗏\mathsf{Ev} in the differential-stage failure domain. By Definition 6.137, law-description operability holds and the full differential-condition bundle does not hold. By Definition 5.132, the set of nodes at which the universal differential condition takes the value false is nonempty.

Because the differential-condition DAG is finite, this set has a minimal element ii with respect to the reachability order. For ii, every ancestor node jj satisfies Kjdiff⁢[𝖤𝗏]K_{j}^{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}]. Indeed, if an ancestor node taking the value false existed, that node would be a false node preceding ii, contrary to the minimality of ii.

Proposition 5.137 gives 𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝖠𝗇𝖼𝖠𝗅𝗅i⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{DiffCondAncAll}_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}]. Because ii is a false node, ¬Kidiff⁢[𝖤𝗏]\neg K_{i}^{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}] also holds. Definition 6.140 then gives 𝖥𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿i⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{FDiff}_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}]. Therefore, 𝖤𝗏\mathsf{Ev} belongs to the union of the differential-stage failure parent regions.

Conversely, for some i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿condi\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}, suppose that 𝖥𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿i⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{FDiff}_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}] holds. Definition 6.140 gives the all-ancestors-satisfied bundle and failure of the ii-th universal differential condition. The all-ancestors-satisfied bundle includes law-description operability, and failure of the ii-th universal differential condition entails failure of the full differential-condition bundle. By Definition 6.137, 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅diff⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{Fail}_{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}] holds. Therefore, 𝖤𝗏\mathsf{Ev} belongs to the differential-stage failure domain.

These two implications establish the set equality and the predicate equivalence for each evaluation specification. ∎

Proposition 6.146 (Antichain property of the simultaneous minimal-failure node set).

For each 𝖤𝗏∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖣𝗈𝗆diff⁢(𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼)\mathsf{Ev}\in\mathsf{FailDom}_{\mathrm{diff}}\left(\mathsf{EvSpec}\right),

𝖬𝗂𝗇𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖨𝖽𝗑diff⁢[𝖤𝗏]\displaystyle\mathsf{MinFailIdx}_{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}]
∈Antichain⁡(I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond,E𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond)∖{∅}.\displaystyle\in\operatorname{Antichain}\left(I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}% }\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak E_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}\right)% \setminus\{\varnothing\}.
Proof.

Let i,j∈𝖬𝗂𝗇𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖨𝖽𝗑diff⁢[𝖤𝗏]i\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak j\in\mathsf{MinFailIdx}_{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf% {Ev}], and suppose that reachability holds from ii to jj. Definition 6.140 gives ¬Kidiff⁢[𝖤𝗏]\neg K_{i}^{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}]. On the other hand, because ii is a strict ancestor of jj, the satisfaction of 𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝖠𝗇𝖼𝖠𝗅𝗅j⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{DiffCondAncAll}_{j}[\mathsf{Ev}] gives Kidiff⁢[𝖤𝗏]K_{i}^{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}], a contradiction. Next suppose that reachability holds from jj to ii. Definition 6.140 gives ¬Kjdiff⁢[𝖤𝗏]\neg K_{j}^{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}]. On the other hand, because jj is a strict ancestor of ii, the satisfaction of 𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝖠𝗇𝖼𝖠𝗅𝗅i⁢[𝖤𝗏]\mathsf{DiffCondAncAll}_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}] gives Kjdiff⁢[𝖤𝗏]K_{j}^{\mathrm{diff}}[\mathsf{Ev}], again a contradiction. Thus the simultaneous minimal-failure node set is an antichain.

Nonemptiness follows from the existence of a minimal element, with respect to the reachability order, in every nonempty set of false nodes on a finite DAG, together with Theorem 6.145. ∎

Remark 6.147 (Dependence of the differential-stage failure-domain cover on the condition family).

The cover in Theorem 6.145 covers the failure domain relative to the five universal differential conditions of Definition 5.130. Each parent region decomposes into the covered region and the unrefined region of Definition 6.143.

Proposition 6.148 (Relative-nonemptiness criterion for differential-stage failure parent regions).

For a set 𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{EvSpec} of complete evaluation specifications, the following are equivalent.

  2. 2.
    ∀i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond,𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖱𝖾𝗀diff,i⁢(𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼)≠∅.\forall i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak% \qquad\mathsf{FailReg}_{\mathrm{diff}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak i}\left(% \mathsf{EvSpec}\right)\neq\varnothing.
  3. 3.

    There exists a family of evaluation specifications

    (𝖤𝗏i)i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond∈∏i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\left(\mathsf{Ev}_{i}\right)_{i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}}\in\prod_% {i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}}\mathsf{EvSpec}

    such that, for each i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿condi\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}, 𝖥𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿i⁢[𝖤𝗏i]\mathsf{FDiff}_{i}[\mathsf{Ev}_{i}] holds.

Proof.

First suppose the first condition holds. Taking an element of the product shows that each coordinate belongs to the corresponding factor. Hence every parent region is nonempty.

Next suppose the second condition holds. For each index in the finite index set, take an evaluation specification from the corresponding nonempty parent region. By Definition 6.142, each evaluation specification belongs to the set of complete evaluation specifications and satisfies the corresponding differential-stage minimal failure condition.

Finally suppose the third condition holds. By Definition 6.142, for each i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿condi\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}, 𝖤𝗏i\mathsf{Ev}_{i} belongs to the corresponding parent region. Therefore, the family of evaluation specifications (𝖤𝗏i)i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond(\mathsf{Ev}_{i})_{i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}} belongs to the product of the family of parent regions, and the first condition holds. ∎

Corollary 6.149 (Finite witness set for differential-stage failure parent regions).

For a set of complete evaluation specifications

𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{EvSpec}

and

(𝖤𝗏i)i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond∈∏i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖱𝖾𝗀diff,i⁢(𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼)\left(\mathsf{Ev}_{i}\right)_{i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}}\in\prod_% {i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}}\mathsf{FailReg}_{\mathrm{diff}% \mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak i}\left(\mathsf{EvSpec}\right)

the set {𝖤𝗏i∣i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond}\{\mathsf{Ev}_{i}\mid i\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}\} has at most five elements, and for each i∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿condi\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}},

{𝖤𝗏j∣j∈I𝖽𝗂𝖿𝖿cond}∩𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖱𝖾𝗀diff,i⁢(𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼)≠∅.\{\mathsf{Ev}_{j}\mid j\in I_{\mathsf{diff}}^{\mathrm{cond}}\}\cap\mathsf{% FailReg}_{\mathrm{diff}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak i}\left(\mathsf{EvSpec}% \right)\neq\varnothing.
Proof.

The product membership in the proposition places the evaluation specification for each index in the corresponding parent region. Each evaluation specification also belongs to the candidate set, so the intersection of each parent region with that candidate set contains the corresponding evaluation specification. The candidate set has at most five elements. ∎

Remark 6.150 (Scope of nonemptiness of differential-stage failure parent regions).

Proposition 6.148 expresses simultaneous nonemptiness of the five parent regions as nonemptiness of the finite witness product. Once evaluation specifications belonging to the respective parent regions have been constructed, the finite witness set in Corollary 6.149 is determined.

For each complete evaluation specification 𝖤𝗏∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼diff\mathsf{Ev}\in\mathsf{EvSpec}^{\mathrm{diff}},

Furthermore,

𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿𝖮𝗉𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗏𝖾⁢[𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖺𝗍]\displaystyle\mathsf{DiffOperative}\left[\mathsf{DiffEvalDat}\right]
⟹𝖫𝖺𝗐𝖮𝗉𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗏𝖾⁢[𝖫𝖺𝗐𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖺𝗍].\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\mathsf{LawOperative}\left[\mathsf{LawEvalDat}% \right].
Proof.

The first implication follows from the equivalence in Proposition 6.139. The second follows from the first component of the conjunction given by Definition 5.132. ∎

Proposition 6.154 (Evaluation targets of the law, approximation, and differential failure series).

The evaluation targets of the three series are given in the following table.

Series Evaluation target
𝖥𝖫\mathsf{FL} Application domain, determinacy, satisfaction, faithful-representation covariance, and simultaneous satisfaction of the general-law relation
𝖥𝖠\mathsf{FA} Quantitative-approximation defect quantities, admissible thresholds, continuous extension, order stability, and relation stability
𝖥𝖣𝗂𝖿𝖿\mathsf{FDiff} Differential-atlas regularity, generated-trajectory jets, local jet relations, and jet-relation covariance

FL3 evaluates membership of a generated trajectory in a general-law relation, whereas FDiff3 evaluates membership of a generated-trajectory jet in a local jet relation. FL4 evaluates preservation of general-law-relation membership under a faithful-representation change, whereas FDiff4 and FDiff5 evaluate preservation of jet-relation membership under a value-chart change and a time-representation change, respectively.

The FA series takes as input the quantitative-evaluation component of 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖨𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍cont⁢[𝖨]\mathsf{EvalInput}^{\mathrm{cont}}[\mathsf{I}], whereas the FDiff series takes as input 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖨𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍diff\mathsf{EvalInput}^{\mathrm{diff}} of Definition 5.136. An implication linking the two series requires a condition that relates the components of the two input types.

Proof.

The evaluation targets of FL3 and FL4 are an element of a general-law relation and a faithful-representation change. The evaluation targets of FDiff3 are the generated-trajectory jet and local jet relation of Definition 5.123. The evaluation targets of FDiff4 and FDiff5 are, respectively, the value-jet-change map of Definition 5.126 and the time-representation-change jet map of Definition 5.128.

The quantitative-evaluation component of the FA series belongs to the continuum-approximation evaluation input of Definition 4.168. The condition DAG, all-ancestors-satisfied bundle, and family of differential-evaluation structures of the FDiff series belong to the differential-stage failure-evaluation input of Definition 5.136. Therefore, the evaluation targets and input types of the respective series follow the distinctions in the table. ∎

Proof.

By Proposition 6.23, membership of a failure token is equivalent to the failed state of that token. By Definition 6.10 and Definition 6.136, this false evaluation value is equivalent to the negation of the ii-th universal differential condition. By the assumption of the all-ancestors-satisfied bundle and Definition 6.140, the conjunction of this negated condition and the all-ancestors-satisfied bundle is equivalent to the ii-th differential-stage minimal-failure class. Applying the equivalences obtained for all indices to the respective components of Definition 6.155 gives the equality between each failure-token membership indicator and the corresponding signature component. ∎

then 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖾𝖽𝖳𝗈𝗄⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]\mathsf{FailedTok}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda] is a singleton and exactly one component of the six-series failure signature has value 1.

|𝖡𝖽𝗋𝗒𝖤𝗑𝖼approx⁢[𝖤𝗏]|≥2.\left|\mathsf{BdryExc}^{\mathrm{approx}}[\mathsf{Ev}]\right|\geq 2.

The first component of the multiplicity report is determined by the cardinality of the structural minimal-position set, and the second component by the cardinality of the excess-component set at the approximation-scale boundary.

For every (𝖤𝗏,λ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ(\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda)\in\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}, the equality of minimal elements in Proposition 6.26 holds.

This cover ranges over the failure tokens of the six series declared in Definition 6.10. The domain of evaluation specifications is 𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}.

Proof.

By the disjoint union in Definition 6.10, each failure token belongs to exactly one series.

Proposition 6.173 (Determinacy and Audit Inputs of the Failure-Localization Results).

The failure-localization data of Definition 6.172 are uniquely determined. Among its three validity scale domains, the full-evaluation validity scale domain equals the intersection of the strict-validity and approximation-validity scale domains. The maximal approximation-validity interval is contained in the approximation-validity scale domain; under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.163, the two are equal.

The first-failure report, multiplicity report, and structural-burden report are uniquely determined. The construction by state evaluation and the construction by minimal failure positions yield the same six-series failure signature. The minimal failure positions are covered relative to the adopted six series and to the evaluation states on the scale-augmented complete evaluation specification.

Proof.

Definition 6.161 and Proposition 6.162 uniquely determine the three validity scale domains and establish their intersection equality. Definition 6.93 uniquely determines the maximal approximation-validity interval and places it within the approximation-validity scale domain. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.163, that theorem gives equality of the two domains.

Theorem 6.164 uniquely determines the first-failure report. Definition 6.165 uniquely determines the multiplicity report. Proposition 6.171 uniquely determines the structural-burden report.

By Proposition 6.160, the construction by state evaluation and the construction by minimal failure positions yield the same six-series failure signature. By Theorem 6.168, the minimal failure positions are covered relative to the adopted six series.

Consequently, the three validity scale domains, maximal approximation-validity interval, first-failure report, multiplicity report, and structural-burden report are uniquely determined, yielding the inputs to the operational audit report. ∎

On the basis of the results of Theorem 4.177, Theorem 5.112, and Theorem 6.164, localize validity, validity domains, the approximation limit, the maximal validity interval, the failure-position token system, and the minimal failure-position set.

Failure positions divide into six groups: the comparison, representation, continuum-approximation, dynamical-description, law-representation, and differential-consistency and law-form-preservation stages. Represent each position by a failure-position token of Definition 6.10. The failed-token set obtained from the evaluation states and the failure-generation dependency order determine the minimal-position representation of the six-series failure signature in Proposition 6.160.

that constitute the audit computation core respectively identify the audit convention, specify the evaluation target and formation states, provide the six-series condition evaluations, and supply the scale order, defect quantities, and admissible thresholds.

By Definition 6.178, the components of the audit computation core are the audit contract, audit input, six-series family of condition evidence, and scale-audit datum.

For each τ∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖾𝗌\tau\in\mathsf{FailSeries} and i∈Iτfaili\in I_{\tau}^{\mathrm{fail}}, the family of condition evidence provides the typed condition evidence corresponding to 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼𝖠𝗍τ⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]\mathsf{FailSpecAt}_{\tau}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda] from the current scale-augmented evaluation specification. The state fibres and indicator functions of Definition 6.179 also uniquely determine the set of indeterminate positions and the indeterminate signature.

Consequently, the four tagged diagnostic components, the audit-state report, the audit-diagnostic report, and the audit report are uniquely determined in sequence. ∎

such that

This isomorphism assigns to the audit-condition state family, six-group audit state, set of audit-undefined reasons, failure-position audit component, failure-signature audit component, set of indeterminate positions, indeterminate signature, approximation-boundary audit component, and structural-burden audit component the correspondences induced by the assumed correspondences.

Proof.

The typed audit-data isomorphism gives isomorphisms of the six failure series, series index sets, failure-position tokens, and failure-generation dependency orders. The roots, immediate predecessors, and linear extensions of the failure-generation dependency orders therefore correspond.

Preservation of the audit contracts, formation-state-augmented audit inputs, and serieswise condition evidence preserves, for each pair of corresponding failure-position tokens, the value recording whether all immediate-predecessor condition states equal 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖯𝖺𝗌𝗌\mathsf{AuditPass}, the formation decision, the condition-evidence satisfaction value, and the condition-evidence failure value. Applying the finite-DAG recursion of Proposition 6.182 to corresponding linear extensions preserves every value of the five-valued audit-condition state of Definition 6.179 between corresponding failure-position tokens.

Because the state-priority order and the failure-position-token set of each series are preserved, 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖦𝗋𝗈𝗎𝗉𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝗎𝗌\mathsf{AuditGroupStatus}, which consists of the serieswise maxima, is also preserved. Because the correspondences between the audit-undefined state values and the failure-position tokens are preserved, they induce the serieswise sets of audit-undefined reasons and the all-series set of audit-undefined reasons.

The correspondence of audit-condition states and failure-position tokens induces the set of failure positions and the set of indeterminate positions. The correspondences of the six series and series index sets induce the failure signature and indeterminate signature.

Preservation of the total scale order, approximation scale, codomains of defect quantities, admissible thresholds, and approximation boundaries induces the approximation-boundary data and approximation-boundary audit component. The isomorphism of failure-generation dependency orders preserves the principal upper set generated by each failure-position token. Together with preservation of the correspondence from failure-position tokens to structural-target tokens, this induces the failure-position-side structural burden, approximation-scale-boundary-side structural burden, and structural-burden audit component.

Combining componentwise the correspondences among the components of the evidence-provenance certificates, the audit-data isomorphism, and the induced correspondences above gives the induced audit-report map stated in the proposition. Each component correspondence is bijective, and its inverse preserves the same structures; hence this map is an isomorphism.

Definition 6.181 determines the audit report from these components. The induced correspondences of the components make this isomorphism satisfy the commutative equation in the proposition.

Each component of the audit report is uniquely determined by the correspondence supplied by the audit-data isomorphism. The induced audit-report isomorphism having the component correspondences above is therefore also unique. ∎

Proposition 6.186 (Finite Audit Procedure with Five-Valued Halting Output).

Take a scale-augmented complete evaluation specification (𝖤𝗏,λ)∈𝖤𝗏𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼Λ(\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda)\in\mathsf{EvSpec}_{\Lambda}. Use the six-failure-series family of evaluation specifications 𝖤𝗏fail\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}} of Definition 6.10. Given the finite operational audit fragment 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖥𝗋𝖺𝗀𝗆𝖾𝗇𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏fail;λ]\mathsf{AuditFragment}[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}};\lambda], there exists an audit procedure that, after finitely many decisions, halts, for every t∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄t\in\mathsf{FailTok}, with exactly one element of 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝗎𝗌\mathsf{AuditStatus}.

From these halting outputs and the approximation-boundary data and structural images retained in the finite operational audit fragment, finitely many set operations, maximum operations, and tagged-component generations yield every component of 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖲𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖱𝖾𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏fail;λ]\mathsf{AuditStateReport}[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}};\lambda] and 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖣𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗇𝗈𝗌𝗍𝗂𝖼𝖱𝖾𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏fail;λ]\mathsf{AuditDiagnosticReport}[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}};\lambda]. If the operational audit datum 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖣𝖺𝗍𝖺⁢[𝖤𝗏fail]\mathsf{AuditData}[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}}] is also supplied, its tuple with these two reports gives 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖱𝖾𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏fail;λ]\mathsf{AuditReport}[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}};\lambda].

Proof.

By Definition 6.10 and Proposition 6.15, 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{FailTok} is a finite set with 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖢𝗈𝗎𝗇𝗍max\mathsf{FailCount}^{\max} elements. By Proposition 6.18, the failure-generation dependency order is a partial order on this finite set. The failure-generation dependency DAG therefore has a finite linear extension.

Process each

t∈𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄t\in\mathsf{FailTok}

along that linear extension. From the finite operational audit fragment, obtain the immediate-predecessor condition-satisfaction value, formation value, evaluation-input satisfaction value, and condition-evaluation value for

𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖠𝗋𝗀𝖠𝗍𝖤𝗏,λ⁢(t).\mathsf{FailArgAt}_{\mathsf{Ev}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\lambda}(t).

Definition 6.21 determines the four-valued evaluation state, and the five-valued lift map of Definition 6.179 determines the audit-condition state. Each processing step consists of finitely many membership, equality, or truth-value decisions and halts in one of the five mutually disjoint cases.

Because the failure-position-token set is finite, generation of all audit-condition states also halts after finitely many decisions. By Proposition 6.182, the resulting state family is unique and is independent of the choice of linear extension.

Each series is a nonempty finite set, and the audit-state priority order is a total order; hence the six-group audit state is obtained by finitely many maximum operations. The set of audit-undefined reasons, set of indeterminate positions, and indeterminate signature are obtained by set comprehensions, a finite union, and indicator functions on the finite state family.

The audit-state report consists of the components obtained above. The condition-state family determines the failure-position set and failure signature. The approximation-boundary data and single-token structural burdens retained in the finite operational audit fragment determine the structural-burden report by finite unions. Applying the tagged audit-result maps of Definition 6.180 to these values and the set of audit-undefined reasons yields every component of the audit-diagnostic report. If the operational audit datum is also supplied, its tuple with these two reports is the audit report of the same definition. ∎

Corollary 6.187 (Five-Valued Operational Auditability of the Time-Reference Formation Conditions).

Given the operational audit datum 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖣𝖺𝗍𝖺⁢[𝖤𝗏fail]\mathsf{AuditData}\left[\mathsf{Ev}^{\mathrm{fail}}\right] and an approximation scale λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, the five-valued audit states of all failure conditions, six-group audit state, set of audit-undefined reasons, failure-position audit component, failure-signature audit component, set of indeterminate positions, indeterminate signature, approximation-boundary audit component, and structural-burden audit component are uniquely determined.

When the corresponding finite operational audit fragment is given, these components are obtained from the halting output of a finite audit procedure together with that fragment. The audit-state and audit-diagnostic reports obtained from two finite operational audit fragments corresponding under a typed audit-data isomorphism correspond under the respective component maps of 𝖠𝗎𝖽𝗂𝗍𝖱𝖾𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍𝖨𝗌𝗈01\mathsf{AuditReportIso}^{01}.

Proof.

By Theorem 6.183, all components of the audit report are uniquely determined by the operational audit datum and approximation scale.

By Proposition 6.186, the condition evaluation for every failure-position token contained in the finite operational audit fragment halts after finitely many decisions with one of the five-valued audit states. By the same proposition, every component of the audit-state and audit-diagnostic reports is obtained from all condition states and the data retained in the finite operational audit fragment by finitely many operations.

By Proposition 6.184, a typed audit-data isomorphism induces a unique audit-report isomorphism. The audit-report isomorphism therefore preserves the component correspondences that depend on the representation of the finite operational audit fragment. ∎

    A requirement for a boundary-handling method has a target token in the continuum-approximation series. For each engineering-measurement reference cited, that boundary treatment is necessary to evaluate the target token. 𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖤𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]\displaystyle\mathsf{EngAuxEffectTarget}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda]
:={t|∃𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖥𝗅𝖺𝗀(0),∃𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖤𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍(0),(𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖥𝗅𝖺𝗀(0),𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖤𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍(0),t)∈𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖤𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝖤𝗏𝗂𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝖾⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]}.\displaystyle\quad:=\Biggl{\{}t\ \Biggm{|}\ \begin{gathered}\exists\mathsf{% EngAuxFlag}^{(0)}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\ \exists\mathsf{EngAuxEffect}^{% (0)}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\\[-2.0pt] (\mathsf{EngAuxFlag}^{(0)}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{EngAuxEffect}^{% (0)}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak t)\in\mathsf{EngAuxEffectEvidence}[\mathsf{% Ev};\lambda]\end{gathered}\Biggr{\}}.

Then 𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖠𝗎𝗑𝖤𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗍⁢[𝖤𝗏;λ]⊆𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{EngAuxEffectTarget}[\mathsf{Ev};\lambda]\subseteq\mathsf{FailTok} .

Proof.

The effect-specific verification conditions in Definition 6.197 give the respective conclusions for unsatisfied formation inputs, unsatisfied evaluation inputs, and requirements for boundary-handling methods. A requirement for exact condition evidence identifies the necessary component within the series evidence data of Definition 6.177. By the candidate type, the third component of each verified item belongs to 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{FailTok}. Its image, the target set, is therefore a subset of 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{FailTok}. ∎

Definition 6.200 (Uses of External Time References).

Let the set of engineering-measurement references that refer to external-time values be 𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍⊆𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗆𝖱𝖾𝖿\mathsf{ExternalTimeRefSet}\subseteq\mathsf{EngParamRef} . Define the type of external-time-reference uses by

𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗒𝗉𝖾\displaystyle\mathsf{ExternalTimeUseType}
:={𝖫𝗈𝗀𝖨𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗑𝖴𝗌𝖾,𝖢𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖻𝗋𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖴𝗌𝖾,𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾,𝖦𝖾𝗇𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖯𝗋𝖾𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾}.\displaystyle:=\left\{\mathsf{LogIndexUse}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\mathsf% {CalibrationUse}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ProvenanceUse}\mathchar 4% 4\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{GeneratedConditionPremiseUse}\right\}.

Let the external-time-reference-use map be

𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾:𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍\displaystyle\mathsf{ExternalTimeUse}:\mathsf{ExternalTimeRefSet}
⟶𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾𝖳𝗒𝗉𝖾.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\mathsf{ExternalTimeUseType}.

For each reference, its use value is 𝖦𝖾𝗇𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖯𝗋𝖾𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾\mathsf{GeneratedConditionPremiseUse} if and only if the audited formation inputs, evaluation inputs, or condition-evaluation expressions contain a use of its external-time value as a premise. Only references without such a use are assigned one of the other three values according to their actual use. Define the set of external-time references producing input-admissibility violations by

𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖵𝗂𝗈𝗅𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍\displaystyle\mathsf{ExternalTimeViolationRefSet}
:={r∈𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍|𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾⁢(r)=𝖦𝖾𝗇𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖯𝗋𝖾𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖴𝗌𝖾}.\displaystyle:=\left\{r\in\mathsf{ExternalTimeRefSet}\ \middle|\ \begin{% aligned} &\mathsf{ExternalTimeUse}\left(r\right)\\ &=\mathsf{GeneratedConditionPremiseUse}\end{aligned}\right\}.
Proposition 6.201 (Noncircularity of Time Generation under External-Time-Reference Audit).

Suppose that 𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖵𝗂𝗈𝗅𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍=∅\mathsf{ExternalTimeViolationRefSet}=\varnothing . Then external-time references belong to the engineering audit input as components of log indexing, instrument calibration, or evidence provenance, while the grounds establishing the comparison conditions, representation conditions, dynamical-description conditions, continuum-approximation conditions, law-representation conditions, and differential-consistency conditions are determined by the typed audit inputs and condition evidence of the respective series.

If, on the other hand,

𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖵𝗂𝗈𝗅𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍≠∅\mathsf{ExternalTimeViolationRefSet}\neq\varnothing

then every

𝖤𝗇𝗀𝖯𝖺𝗋𝖺𝗆𝖱𝖾𝖿(0)∈𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖵𝗂𝗈𝗅𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍\mathsf{EngParamRef}^{(0)}\in\mathsf{ExternalTimeViolationRefSet}

identifies a use as a generation-condition premise corresponding to

𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍𝖺𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖥𝗅𝖺𝗀,\mathsf{ExternalTimeContaminationFlag}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak

and provides evidence for

𝖨𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍𝖠𝖽𝗆𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗂𝖻𝗂𝗅𝗂𝗍𝗒𝖵𝗂𝗈𝗅𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖤𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍.\mathsf{InputAdmissibilityViolationEffect}.
Proof.

The use map in Definition 6.200 preserves whether an external-time value is actually used as a generation-condition premise. Consider its four use cases.

For log-index use, the external-time value identifies an engineering-measurement record. For instrument-calibration use, the external-time value is used in an engineering-measurement component accompanied by a calibration provenance. For evidence-provenance use, the external-time value is used in components recording evidence location and transformation history. In these three uses, the six-series condition states are determined from the formation-input satisfaction values, evaluation-input satisfaction values, and condition-evaluation values of Definition 6.179.

For generated-condition-premise use, an external-time value occurs in the grounds establishing a formation input, evaluation input, or condition-evaluation expression of one of the six series. A reference having this use belongs to 𝖤𝗑𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗇𝖺𝗅𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾𝖵𝗂𝗈𝗅𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖿𝖲𝖾𝗍\mathsf{ExternalTimeViolationRefSet} and identifies the use corresponding to the external-time-contamination flag of Definition 6.195. By Table 14, the evidence for an input-admissibility violation is this use as a generation-condition premise.

Consequently, when the violation set is empty, the six-series condition states are determined from the typed audit inputs and condition evidence of the respective series. When the violation set is nonempty, each element identifies a use that violates input admissibility. ∎

Definition 6.202 (Engineering Formal-Condition Evidence).

Proposition 6.206 (Separation of Engineering-Evidence-Relative Structural Burdens for Bulk-Recording and Following-Recording Types).

The two structural burdens are subsets of 𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖼𝗍𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{StructTok}, and

𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇bulk=𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇follow⟺𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇△=∅.\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{\mathrm{bulk}}=\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{\mathrm{follow}}% \Longleftrightarrow\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{\triangle}=\varnothing.

For each a∈{0,1}a\in\{0\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak 1\}, if some t∈𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖳𝗈𝗄(a)t\in\mathsf{RecordBurdenTok}^{(a)} satisfies

𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖼𝗍𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇⁢({t})⊈𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇(1−a)\mathsf{StructBurden}(\{t\})\not\subseteq\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{(1-a)}

then

𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇(a)∖𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇(1−a)≠∅.\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{(a)}\setminus\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{(1-a)}\neq\varnothing.

If this condition holds for both a=0a=0 and a=1a=1, the two structural burdens are incomparable under inclusion.

Proof.

The set of failure positions for each recording configuration is a subset of 𝖥𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{FailTok}. By Definition 6.169, each 𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇(a)\mathsf{RecordBurden}^{(a)} is therefore a subset of 𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖼𝗍𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathsf{StructTok}. Applying the equivalence between emptiness of the symmetric difference and equality of two sets to the two structural burdens yields the first equivalence.

For each a∈{0,1}a\in\{0\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak 1\}, nonemptiness of the set difference follows by applying Lemma 6.170 to

A=𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖳𝗈𝗄(a),B=𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽𝖡𝗎𝗋𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖳𝗈𝗄(1−a)A=\mathsf{RecordBurdenTok}^{(a)}\mathchar 44\relax\allowbreak\qquad B=\mathsf{% RecordBurdenTok}^{(1-a)}

Nonemptiness of the set difference in both directions establishes that the two structural burdens are incomparable under inclusion. ∎
